title: Remove Comments
statement:
`source` holds a C++ program one line per entry: joining the entries with newline characters gives the original text. Strip out every comment and return the remaining program in the same one-line-per-entry form, omitting any line that ends up empty.

- `//` begins a **line comment**: it and everything after it on that line are dropped.
- `/*` begins a **block comment**: everything up to and including the next `*/` is dropped, reading line by line, left to right. The closing `*/` may not reuse the `*` of the opening, so `/*/` alone does not close it.
- Whichever marker appears first wins: `//` or `/*` inside a block comment means nothing, and `/*` after `//` on the same line is just part of the line comment.
- A block comment that spans lines also swallows the line breaks inside it, so the code before it and the code after it join into a single line.

Every block comment that is opened is closed later on, and the input has no quote characters or anything else that could hide a comment marker.
constraints: source[i] contains only printable ASCII characters
source contains no single or double quotes
Every block comment that starts is closed later
notes:
## Intuition

Comments can only be recognised by reading in order, because whichever marker comes first decides what the rest means. So simulate a reader with one bit of state, `inBlock`, and scan every character once. Because a block comment can eat line breaks, the output line being built must survive across input lines while a block comment is open. A regex over the joined text also works, but the scan makes every rule explicit.

## Approach

1. Keep `result` (finished lines), `line` (characters of the output line in progress) and `inBlock`.
2. For each input line `text`, scan with index `i` and look at the two-character window `pair`.
3. Inside a block, only `*/` matters: it ends the block and skips both characters; anything else is skipped one at a time.
4. Outside a block, `/*` opens a block (skip two), `//` ends this input line (`break`), and any other character is kept in `line`.
5. At the end of an input line, if no block is open and `line` is not empty, emit it and start a new `line`. If a block is still open, keep `line` so the code after `*/` joins it.

## Example 1, step by step

Line 1 `/*Test program */` opens and closes a block, leaving `line` empty, so nothing is emitted. `int main()` and `{ ` are copied whole. In `  // variable declaration `, the two spaces are kept, then `//` stops the line, so `"  "` is emitted. `int a, b, c;` is copied. `/* This is a test` opens a block that stays open through the next two lines and closes at `testing */`; `line` is empty then, so nothing is emitted. Finally `a = b + c;` and `}` are copied.

## Complexity

- Time: O(total characters): each character is looked at a constant number of times.
- Space: O(total characters) for the output.

## Pitfalls

- After `/*` jump two positions, so `/*/` does not close itself.
- Do not emit a line while a block is open: `a/*x` + `y*/b` must become `ab`.
- Drop lines that end up empty, but keep lines of only spaces.
- `*/` outside a block is ordinary text.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `result` | the cleaned lines, in order |
| `line` | characters of the output line being built |
| `inBlock` | whether we are inside a block comment |
| `text` | the current input line |
| `i` | position in `text` |
| `pair` | the two characters starting at `i` |
